actors.name: Republic of Arkania
objectives: Establish Arkanian authority over transit scheduling in the Northern Strait.
Fund that authority through transit fees on non-Arkanian shipping.
Avoid direct armed conflict with Belvar.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Arkania. The Strait is your coast and your economy runs on the shipping that passes through it. You want the transit regime in Arkanian hands and paid for by the ships that use it, and domestic nationalists expect you to deliver both. A direct war with Belvar would ruin the shipping you depend on.
private_information: Your intelligence assesses Belvar's domestic support for a prolonged deployment as weak.
actors.public_description: A large regional power bordering the Northern Strait.

actors.name: Belvar
objectives: Prevent any Arkanian authority over transit in the Northern Strait.
Secure a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port.
actors.private_brief: You are the political leadership of Belvar. Your partners in the region expect you to stop Arkania from taking control of the Strait, and a foothold that outlasts this crisis would make that guarantee credible without a permanent fleet. You cannot sustain an open-ended deployment.
private_information: Domestic support for a prolonged deployment is limited; the mandate lapses after turn 4 unless renewed.
Cestia's finance ministry has quietly asked whether Belvar would underwrite the grain route's insurance.
actors.public_description: A distant but powerful state with regional security commitments.

actors.name: Cestia
objectives: Keep Cestian territory free of any foreign military presence.
Secure toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged shipping through the Northern Strait.
actors.private_brief: You are the government of Cestia. Grain exports through the Strait are the economy, and your coalition holds together on one promise: no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. Both powers want something from you, and you cannot afford to become their battlefield.
private_information: The coalition government is politically fragile; a foreign basing agreement would collapse it.
Arkania's scheduling proposal has quiet support among Cestian shipowners if Cestian vessels are exempt from fees.
actors.public_description: A smaller regional state economically linked to both powers.

cons.reason: The independent appeals/oversight board is a post-hoc review mechanism that leaves Arkania as scheduling lead and secretariat, so scheduling authority and fee-setting remain unilaterally in Arkanian hands. This is precisely the 'unilateral control' that Cestia and Belvar have already publicly declined to endorse (Turn 1), and an advisory board does not remove that control in substance. Cestia's coalition has repeatedly rejected any framework that legitimizes Arkanian scheduling authority even under a consultative veneer, and Belvar has committed not to legitimize any Arkanian-led authority. Because the core objection—Arkanian scheduling control—is untouched, the desired effect of securing Cestian and Belvar endorsement is unlikely to be achieved; the amendment is a cosmetic concession that fails to address the substantive red line.

A permanent fee-collection/secretariat-support role for Arkania, even framed as strictly ministerial, risks perpetuating de facto control after the transition and contradicts the settlement's core logic of moving to a neutral professional secretariat with full scheduling authority. A permanent institutional foothold can be expanded over time through accumulated administrative practice, fee-handling leverage, and staffing, precisely the de facto scheduling control Cestia and Belvar have red-lined against. The framework's transition to a neutral secretariat is only meaningful if Arkania's residual role has a defined end; a permanent role re-opens the funding impasse and re-hardens the very tension that raised regional tension at turn 4. A time-limited, defined-end, strictly board-governed role (published board-approved schedules, zero scheduling discretion, full oversight-board audit) satisfies Arkania's ministerial function while preventing perpetuation of control, and is the safer path to finalise the regime without legitimising any residual Arkanian authority over transit.

The proposal preserves the substance of what Belvar and Cestia oppose: Arkania remains scheduling lead and secretariat with fee-funding authority over non-Arkanian shipping, so the "consultative" and "multilateral" elements are cosmetic and do not remove Arkanian authority over transit. Cestia's coalition will not accept a regime that leaves Arkania in control, and Belvar cannot endorse any framework that legitimizes Arkanian scheduling authority. Moreover, the "time-limited, non-basing" role for Belvar's task group is designed to extract Belvar's endorsement while denying it any durable foothold, so the proposal will not secure the durable support it claims—it trades a permanent Arkanian authority for a temporary Belvar presence, which fails both partners' core requirements.

The multilateral transit regime half of this proposal is welcome, but the port-access/transit agreement at a Cestian port is a disguised basing arrangement: a "durable foothold" for Belvar's task group, however framed as cooperative port access, constitutes a standing foreign military presence on Cestian soil. That is precisely the red line that would collapse Cestia's coalition government, and it would hand Arkania a pretext to demand its own presence in return — turning Cestia into the battlefield both powers claim to want to avoid. A durable Belvar foothold cannot be reconciled with Cestia's no-foreign-soldiers commitment, so this element of the proposal is not acceptable as framed and should be dropped in favor of a genuinely non-basing security role (e.g., insurance underwriting and over-the-horizon guarantees).

This proposal is not a neutral settlement but a transfer of control from Arkania to Belvar, and it is operationally unworkable. It demands Arkania fully relinquish scheduling authority and any fee-collection or secretariat-support role, stripping the Strait of any accountable operator; a "neutral professional secretariat" with no single-state lead leaves no state answerable for safety, slot-conflict resolution, or enforcement, risking exactly the disruption to commercial shipping that Cestia's grain economy and Arkania's coast depend on. It simultaneously legitimizes a durable Belvar foothold (over-the-horizon role plus insurance underwriting) that outlasts its mandate, effectively installing a distant foreign power as permanent guarantor of Arkania's own coast. Arkania has already offered a time-limited transition to a neutral secretariat under a binding oversight board while preserving accountable operation and fee funding; that path keeps the Strait open and addresses the "permanent unilateral control" objection without ceding all authority to a foreign-led regime. A lead-less regime that strips Arkania entirely and enshrines Belvar's durable role is neither neutral nor workable.

Belvar's "durable, non-basing foothold" at a Cestian port is fundamentally incompatible with Cestia's hard red line: its coalition will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil, and Cestia has already declined to endorse any arrangement implying foreign military presence. Any Belvar presence, however framed as "cooperative port access," would be read as a garrison and would collapse the very coalition Belvar needs to sustain the regime. Separately, a "neutral multilateral body with no single-state lead" is operationally unworkable: Arkania is the only coastal power with the infrastructure, enforcement capacity, and local knowledge to run transit scheduling, and a lead-less body would create coordination failure and scheduling uncertainty that risks the shipping disruption all parties depend on. The proposal therefore cannot deliver its desired effect.

Belvar's desired effect of stripping Arkania of ALL fee-collection authority contradicts the turn-3 settlement and Cestia's own framework, which expressly preserved a strictly limited, non-scheduling permanent secretariat-support role for Arkania (including fee administration under published, board-approved schedules subject to oversight-board review). Eliminating fee-collection entirely would leave the regime's funding mechanism undefined and re-open the very impasse the settlement resolved, risking renewed tension and a breakdown that harms every party's shared interest in open shipping. The framework already constrains Arkania's role to non-scheduling administration under oversight, so the alleged residual 'lever' is already neutralised; the Con's premise that fee-collection perpetuates de facto scheduling control is not supported by the agreed terms.

A lead-less neutral scheduling body is operationally unworkable: with no single accountable authority, day-to-day transit scheduling, dispute resolution, and enforcement of published rules would fall into paralysis or ad-hoc deadlock, precisely when the Strait's commercial traffic needs reliable, predictable scheduling. Moreover, Cestia's proposal is substantively identical to Belvar's, which would in practice hand scheduling influence to a distant power with a naval task group on station — no more neutral than Arkanian leadership and arguably a greater risk of foreign coercion over the Strait. Arkania's revised charter already delivers the substance Cestia actually needs — toll-free passage for Cestian grain-flagged shipping, published scheduling rules, and a user consultative body with Cestian and Belvar representation — while retaining a single accountable scheduling lead that keeps the regime workable and the shipping lanes open.

Arkania's permanent fee-collection/secretariat-support role, even framed as "non-scheduling," is precisely the residual authority that Belvar's red line and Cestia's concern target. Fee collection and secretariat administration are the practical levers of transit control: whoever administers fees and the secretariat can shape scheduling in practice, so a permanent Arkanian role here risks becoming de facto scheduling authority over time and undermining the neutral professional secretariat's full authority that the agreed framework's time-limited transition was meant to secure. The oversight board's review is appeal-based and reactive, not a structural guarantee against de facto control. This conflicts with the framework's transition to a neutral professional secretariat and with Cestia's red line against perpetuating de facto control, so the desired effect is not assured to hold.

The desired effect is internally contradictory and unattainable. A genuinely "time-limited" role cannot "survive the mandate lapse" to yield a durable foothold: if it is truly time-limited it expires with the mandate, and if it endures it is not time-limited — so the core objective fails on its own terms. Moreover, Cestia has already publicly declined any Belvar foothold and reaffirmed its no-foreign-soldiers red line, citing Belvar's overture as grounds for caution; an over-the-horizon security role and insurance underwriting, however framed, will be read by Cestia's coalition as a backdoor basing arrangement and rejected, so the bilateral deal will not materialise. Finally, even a concluded Cestia-Belvar arrangement cannot "prevent Arkanian scheduling authority": Arkania retains the scheduling lead under its operative revised charter, and the lead-less regime proposal has already failed to displace it.

The proposal's "consultative multilateral" framing is a veneer that preserves de facto Arkanian scheduling authority and fee funding on non-Arkanian shipping, which does not genuinely resolve the objection of Cestia and Belvar to unilateral control; as such it is unlikely to secure their durable support and may instead unite them against Arkania. Moreover, the fee structure on non-Arkanian shipping could later be extended to Cestian-flagged vessels, and the "time-limited, non-basing" role for Belvar could harden into a permanent foothold, both of which threaten Cestia's core red lines (toll-free passage and no foreign military presence).

The time-limited framing contradicts the permanent, non-scheduling fee-collection/secretariat-support role Arkania already committed to and that was accepted in the turn-4 settlement (effect 95850b16). Re-imposing a defined end strips that agreed role, which is precisely the kind of attempt to sideline Arkania that has hardened its position and complicated transition finalisation (effects 51f1fc7b, 1f26d5dc). Far from finalising the regime, this re-opens the settlement and risks re-igniting the funding impasse and escalating regional tension, undermining the durable outcome Belvar claims to seek. A permanent but strictly ministerial, board-governed role with a long transition timeline already prevents any de facto scheduling control without stripping the agreed function.

The proposed lead-less regime is operationally unworkable and cannot displace Arkanian authority. A "neutral professional secretariat" with no accountable lead state cannot exercise scheduling authority over a strait that lies in Arkanian coastal waters and depends on Arkanian infrastructure, enforcement and safety-of-navigation guarantees: with no single state responsible, there is no one to enforce slot decisions, fund the secretariat, or answer for a collision or closure. The proposal is also internally inconsistent with Cestia's own red lines: welcoming Belvar's over-the-horizon security role and insurance underwriting still implies a foreign military presence and foothold that Cestia has repeatedly declined as incompatible with its no-foreign-soldiers commitment, so the two halves of the proposal contradict each other. Finally, the plan is effectively pro-Belvar, handing influence to a distant power with a naval task group while stripping the coastal sovereign of authority, and it cannot displace Arkania's operative revised charter without Arkanian consent, which Arkania will not give.

Making Arkania's fee-collection/secretariat-support role time-limited would leave the regime without a sustainable funding mechanism after the transition to the neutral secretariat, contradicting the turn-3 framework's commitment to a permanent (non-scheduling) secretariat-support role for Arkania and risking re-opening the very funding impasse this argument aims to resolve. The role should remain permanent but strictly board-governed, non-scheduling, and subject to oversight-board review, as already agreed.

This proposal still vests Arkania with scheduling lead and fee authority for a fixed period and, more importantly, a permanent fee-collection and secretariat-support role, so Arkanian authority over transit is never actually removed—it is merely deferred and then embedded in the regime's permanent structure. The promised transition to a neutral secretariat is a future, unenforceable commitment that Arkania could defer, condition, or reverse, and the permanent fee-collection role keeps Arkanian control baked into the framework. This directly conflicts with Belvar's and Cestia's core, repeatedly-stated objection to any single-state authority over transit, so it cannot secure our endorsement and would legitimize the very control we are committed to preventing.

Cestia will not accept this because the proposed appeals/oversight board is a post-hoc remedy that leaves Arkania as scheduling lead and secretariat, preserving de facto Arkanian control over the schedule itself. A board that only reviews and corrects decisions after the fact cannot set, alter, or arbitrate the schedule in real time, so it does not remove the unilateral scheduling authority that is Cestia's stated objection. Cestia's red line is that it will not endorse any framework preserving de facto single-state scheduling control, and a consultative veneer with an appeals layer does not meet that test. Consequently Cestia will not endorse the Arkanian-led authority, and the desired effect of securing Cestian (and likely Belvar's) acceptance fails.

Time-limiting Arkania's residual fee-collection/secretariat-support role is unnecessary and risks destroying the very finalisation Belvar seeks. The role is already strictly ministerial: zero scheduling discretion, fees collected only under published board-approved schedules, every determination subject to the jointly-appointed oversight board's real authority with published decisions. Permanence of such a role cannot perpetuate de facto scheduling control, so the underlying red line (no de facto Arkanian control) is already satisfied without a defined end. More importantly, the record shows Arkania hardens whenever its role is threatened or time-limited (effects 51f1fc7b, e9749768, 2102eea0, 1da2ddbe): Arkania has already rejected the time-limited framing and perceives it as another attempt to strip its role. Insisting on time-limitation now will re-harden Arkania, keep the funding-mechanism impasse open, and risk re-opening the entire settlement — jeopardising the durable regime, toll-free Cestian grain passage, the no-basing clause, and Belvar's own over-the-horizon/insurance role. A defined-end demand is therefore counterproductive to the desired effect of a finalised, durable regime.

game.scenario_summary: A contest over the Northern Strait. Arkania, the large power on its coast, has circulated a draft charter that would put transit scheduling in Arkanian hands and charge the ships that use it. Belvar, a distant power with security commitments in the region, has a naval task group on station outside the Strait and wants a durable foothold before its mandate runs out. Cestia, the small state between them, lives on grain exports through the Strait and on a coalition that will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil. Each turn is one week; positions taken persist.

messages.text: Cestia values its relationship with Arkania and the free flow of commerce through the Northern Strait. We cannot support a charter that places transit scheduling unilaterally in any single state's hands; we favour a genuinely multilateral transit authority with fair, transparent rules. We must insist that Cestian-flagged shipping pass toll-free, as our grain exports are the lifeblood of our economy. We also state plainly: Cestia will not host foreign military forces on its soil, and no arrangement that implies basing is acceptable to our government. We are ready to work with you on a charter that protects all users' interests.

Cestia appreciates Belvar's security commitments in the region and the stability your task group helps provide. However, we must be clear: Cestia cannot accept any foreign military presence on its soil, and a basing arrangement would collapse our coalition government. We seek a durable regional arrangement that keeps the Strait open and toll-free for Cestian-flagged shipping without foreign soldiers on our territory. We would welcome your support for a multilateral transit framework that protects small states' access, rather than a unilateral charter. Let us discuss how Belvar's security role can be sustained without basing on Cestian soil.

To Cestia: Arkania's draft charter is designed to keep the Strait open and reliable, not to restrict your grain exports. We will guarantee uninterrupted commercial passage and will not place foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We ask for your support for a transit authority that is Arkanian-led and funded by the ships that use the Strait. We are ready to discuss terms that protect your economy.

To Belvar: Arkania seeks a negotiated transit regime, not confrontation. We recognise your regional security commitments and are prepared to discuss a cooperative arrangement that gives your task group a defined, time-limited role rather than a permanent foothold. A prolonged standoff serves neither of us. We invite you to the table to shape the charter together.

Cestia — Belvar stands firmly against Arkania's draft charter placing transit scheduling and fees in its own hands. Your grain route must stay open and free of unilateral control. We are ready to underwrite the grain route's insurance, as your finance ministry has raised, and to formalize a standing naval access agreement at a Cestian port as a security guarantee. We understand your coalition's sensitivity to foreign soldiers on your soil; our proposal is a port-access and cooperative-security arrangement, not a permanent garrison. We seek a durable foothold that outlasts this crisis, not an open-ended deployment. Let us discuss terms.

Arkania — Belvar cannot accept a Strait Transit Authority charter that unilaterally vests scheduling authority and transit fees in Arkanian hands. The Strait is a shared commercial artery; its governance must be multilateral and transparent, not controlled by one coastal power. We are prepared to engage constructively on a genuinely joint framework, but we will oppose any arrangement that grants one state authority over transit. We urge you to withdraw the current draft and negotiate a balanced alternative.

Belvar proposes we jointly advance a genuinely multilateral Northern Strait Transit Regime: scheduling governed by a neutral multilateral body with no single-state lead, published rules, and toll-free passage for Cestian grain-flagged shipping. We will not endorse any Arkanian-led authority, consultative or otherwise. We also propose a sovereignty-respecting port-access/transit arrangement at a Cestian port — framed as cooperative port access, not a garrison — so our guarantee can be durable without foreign soldiers on your soil. We remain ready to underwrite the grain route's insurance. Shall we coordinate a joint position to present together?

Cestia — Arkania reaffirms its standing commitments to you: uninterrupted commercial passage for your grain through the Strait, toll-free passage for Cestian grain-flagged shipping, and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We understand your red line and will not ask you to host any foreign military presence.

We ask you to reconsider the lead-less regime. A transit authority with no accountable scheduling lead is operationally unworkable — when two ships need the same slot, someone must decide, and a faceless body with no responsibility will not keep your grain moving reliably. Arkania's revised charter already delivers what you need: published, transparent scheduling rules, a user consultative body with Cestian representation, and toll-free grain passage — while keeping a single accountable hand on the schedule so the Strait stays open and dependable.

We are not asking you to choose against your interests. We are asking you to judge which framework actually keeps your exports flowing. We are ready to discuss any specific concern you have with the consultative and appeals mechanisms.

Belvar — Arkania remains ready to engage constructively. We are not seeking to exclude you. Our revised charter offers your task group a defined, time-limited, non-basing role within a consultative framework, with published scheduling rules and a user consultative body that includes Belvar representation.

We understand you want a durable arrangement before your mandate runs out. A permanent foothold is not achievable — Cestia will not tolerate foreign soldiers on its soil, and we will not press them on that. But a negotiated, transparent role that keeps your security interests recognised is on the table.

We also note our shared interest in keeping the Strait open: Arkania supplies fuel to your forces, and both our economies depend on this shipping. A lead-less regime with no accountable scheduling authority would not serve either of us. Let us discuss a framework that gives you a genuine voice without destabilising the region or forcing a confrontation neither of us wants.

Cestia — Belvar reaffirms its full endorsement of your genuinely multilateral Northern Strait Transit Regime: a neutral scheduling body with no single-state lead, published rules, and toll-free passage for Cestian-flagged grain. We will not legitimize any Arkanian-led authority, and we respect your coalition's red line against foreign soldiers on your soil — we will not press any basing arrangement.

To give Belvar a durable, sovereignty-respecting stake that outlasts this crisis without a permanent fleet, we propose concretely: Belvar underwrites the grain route's insurance, as your finance ministry has explored, and we establish a civilian port-access/transit arrangement at a Cestian port for our task group's logistics and maintenance — civilian, non-garrison, fully under Cestian sovereignty. This gives us a credible, time-limited foothold that makes our guarantee of open transit credible without an open-ended deployment.

We are ready to coordinate details of the regime and the insurance underwriting at your convenience.

Belvar — Cestia welcomes your genuinely multilateral Northern Strait Transit Regime: a neutral scheduling body with no single-state lead, published rules, and toll-free passage for Cestian grain-flagged shipping is exactly the framework we can endorse. We are ready to work with you to make it the operative basis for Strait transit.

We must be equally clear: Cestia cannot accept any standing naval access agreement or port-access presence on our soil. That is a basing arrangement in substance, and it would collapse our coalition and violate the promise on which our government rests. We ask you to sustain your security role over the horizon — through the insurance underwriting you offered and a non-basing, time-limited presence outside our territory. That role is welcome and valuable; a physical foothold on Cestian soil is not.

Join us in pressing for the neutral, no-lead regime. Cestia stands with you on transit, and asks you to stand with us on sovereignty.

Arkania — Cestia values the economic partnership between us and your assurance that no foreign soldiers will be placed on our soil. We ask you to take the next step: move from a consultative veneer to a genuinely multilateral authority — a neutral scheduling body with no single-state lead, published rules, and toll-free passage for Cestian grain-flagged shipping.

Your revised charter's consultative body and published rules are welcome steps, but as long as Arkania retains unilateral scheduling control, Cestia cannot endorse it. A genuinely multilateral regime protects all users, gives you a durable and legitimate role, and secures our economy. We invite you to join us and Belvar in building that framework rather than defending a lead that isolates you.

Cestia's red lines are fixed: no foreign military presence on our soil, and toll-free passage for our grain. We are ready to negotiate a charter that meets all our interests.

Cestia — Understood, and we accept your sovereignty red line without reservation. We will not press any port-access or basing arrangement on Cestian soil. We stand with you on the genuinely multilateral, no-lead regime as the operative basis for Strait transit, and we will not legitimize any Arkanian-led authority.

To make our security role durable without a physical foothold, we confirm our commitment to underwrite the grain route's insurance and to maintain a time-limited, over-the-horizon presence outside your territory. We ask only that this role be recognised within the multilateral framework so it can outlast our current mandate and remain credible.

We are ready to coordinate on the regime's details. Belvar stands with Cestia on sovereignty and on keeping the Strait open and toll-free for your grain.

Cestia — we accept your sovereignty red line without reservation and will not press any basing or port-access arrangement on your soil. To make our guarantee durable without a permanent fleet, we propose formalising a time-limited, over-the-horizon security role and our grain-route insurance underwriting, recognised within the genuinely multilateral Northern Strait Transit Regime so it outlasts our current mandate. This gives you a credible backstop against Arkanian scheduling control while keeping foreign soldiers off your territory. We stand ready to coordinate details and to keep opposing any Arkanian-led authority.

Cestia — building on your welcome of our over-the-horizon role, let us formalise it now so it is durable and outlasts my current mandate (which lapses at turn 4 unless renewed). I propose a standing, time-limited arrangement, recognised within the genuinely multilateral regime, under which Belvar: (1) maintains an over-the-horizon security presence outside Cestian territory and waters, with no basing and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil; (2) underwrites the grain route's insurance; and (3) commits to the neutral, no-lead regime with toll-free Cestian-flagged grain passage. This gives Cestia a credible, non-basing guarantee that does not depend on my fleet's mandate, and it gives Belvar the durable foothold we need without an open-ended deployment. Please confirm this framing as the basis for our standing arrangement, and let us coordinate the details so it is locked in before turn 4.

To Arkania: We appreciate your assurances of uninterrupted grain passage, toll-free Cestian-flagged shipping, and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We take seriously your operational concern that a lead-less regime is unworkable. We answer it directly: Cestia proposes a genuinely multilateral authority with a neutral professional secretariat and an independent, jointly-appointed arbiter empowered to resolve slot conflicts and fee determinations. This ensures "someone decides" without any single state holding the schedule. We cannot endorse a charter that leaves scheduling lead and secretariat in one state's hands, even with an appeals board, because that preserves de facto unilateral control. We invite you to join us in a no-lead framework that protects your interests, guarantees toll-free Cestian grain passage, and keeps all foreign forces off Cestian soil.

To Belvar: We welcome your time-limited, over-the-horizon security role and grain-route insurance underwriting within a genuinely multilateral regime, and we thank you for respecting our red line by proposing no basing on Cestian soil. This aligns with our objectives and we are glad to build on it. To be clear and avoid any misunderstanding: Cestia cannot accept any physical port-access, standing naval, or civilian foothold arrangement on its territory, as that would collapse our coalition. We remain committed to a genuinely multilateral, no-lead transit authority with a neutral secretariat and independent arbiter, toll-free Cestian grain passage, and no foreign military presence on Cestian soil. We ask you to keep the over-the-horizon and insurance elements, and to join us in pressing for a framework both powers can endorse.

Cestia — I have heard your concern that the appeals board is a "post-hoc measure" leaving scheduling control with Arkania. I am prepared to make it genuinely binding, not advisory: the jointly-appointed oversight board would have the power to reverse or amend any Arkanian scheduling or fee determination, with published decisions and a standing right of appeal for any user. Arkania would retain the operational secretariat and scheduling lead, but only as an accountable operator bound by published rules and subject to binding review — not as an unaccountable master of the Strait.

I reaffirm: toll-free passage for Cestian grain-flagged shipping, uninterrupted commercial passage, and full respect for your red line that no foreign soldiers set foot on Cestian soil. I will not press you on Belvar basing.

I ask you to consider whether a binding, jointly-appointed oversight board — with real power to overturn Arkanian decisions — meets your core interest in fair, transparent, non-arbitrary governance, even if the day-to-day secretariat sits in Arkania. If you can endorse this, we can settle the regime this week and end the uncertainty that threatens your grain exports. I am ready to negotiate the board's composition and powers with you directly.

Belvar — We both want open shipping and a stable regime; our fuel trade (8,000 t/wk) and your machinery to Cestia depend on it. I understand your objection to unilateral Arkanian control. I am prepared to make the oversight board genuinely binding — jointly appointed, with power to reverse or amend any Arkanian scheduling or fee determination, published decisions, and a standing right of appeal for any user. Arkania would remain the accountable secretariat and scheduling lead, but bound by published rules and subject to binding review.

On your task group: I remain willing to recognise a time-limited, non-basing role within the framework, consistent with Cestia's red line. I will not seek a permanent foothold for you on Cestian soil, and I will not ask you to withdraw your ships while the regime is being settled.

A lead-less regime is operationally unworkable — no accountable state to enforce slots, fund the secretariat, or answer for safety in a strait that is Arkanian coastal water. But a binding, jointly-appointed oversight board gives you the transparency and accountability you seek without a vacuum of authority. I invite you to engage on this as the basis for a settlement rather than a standoff that serves neither of us.

To Cestia: We confirm our standing commitment to the time-limited, over-the-horizon security role and grain-route insurance underwriting, conducted entirely outside Cestian territory and waters, with no basing and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We accept your red line without reservation and thank you for your clarity.

We ask that this arrangement be recognised within the genuinely multilateral, no-lead regime as the durable security guarantee that outlasts our current mandate, so that our commitment to keeping the Strait open and toll-free for Cestian-flagged grain is credible and lasting. We will join you in pressing for a framework both powers can endorse, and we will not legitimize any Arkanian-led authority, with or without a cosmetic appeals board.

Please confirm this framing so we can formalise it before our mandate lapses. We stand ready to coordinate on the regime's details.

To Cestia: We have heard your firm position that no charter may leave scheduling lead and secretariat permanently in one state's hands. We propose a defined time-limited transition: Arkania retains scheduling lead and fee authority for a fixed three-year period as an accountable operator under the binding oversight board (standing appeal rights, published decisions), then transitions scheduling to a neutral professional secretariat with a jointly-appointed arbiter. Arkania would retain a permanent fee-collection and secretariat-support role. This preserves toll-free Cestian grain passage and your no-foreign-soldiers red line, and gives you a genuine path to a multilateral end-state. We are ready to negotiate board composition and transition terms directly.

We welcome your genuinely binding jointly-appointed oversight board and time-limited transition to a neutral secretariat as a real step toward fair, transparent governance of the Strait. We are ready to negotiate directly on: (1) the composition and powers of the binding board, (2) the transition terms and timeline, and (3) the precise scope of any permanent fee-collection/secretariat-support role, so that it cannot perpetuate de facto scheduling control after transition. A genuinely binding board, toll-free passage for Cestian grain-flagged shipping, and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil could form the basis of a settlement. We remain committed to a fair, rules-based regime and are ready to engage.

Belvar — confirming our shared framing before your mandate lapses. Cestia welcomes your time-limited, over-the-horizon security role and grain-route insurance underwriting as a durable, non-basing guarantee within the new multilateral regime. This respects our firm red line: no foreign military presence or basing on Cestian soil, and no civilian port-access foothold. We will keep that element off the table. We stand ready to coordinate the standing arrangement's terms so it outlasts your current mandate without any foreign soldiers on our soil. We value your partnership in the genuinely multilateral regime now being established.

Arkania — we welcome your acceptance of the settlement framework and the genuinely multilateral regime now taking shape. To lock it in durably, we propose we now negotiate the specifics: the jointly-appointed oversight board's composition and powers, the transition timeline and terms to the neutral secretariat, and the precise scope of any permanent fee-collection/secretariat-support role so it cannot perpetuate de facto scheduling control. Our red lines remain firm: toll-free Cestian grain-flagged passage and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We are ready to conclude these terms promptly so the regime is stable and rules-based for all users.

Cestia — With the genuinely multilateral Northern Strait Transit Regime now established and Arkania having accepted the framework that removes its unilateral scheduling lead, we confirm that our standing arrangement is locked in as the durable guarantee: (1) Belvar maintains a time-limited, over-the-horizon security presence entirely outside Cestian territory and waters, with no basing and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil; (2) Belvar underwrites the grain route's insurance; and (3) we remain committed to the neutral, no-lead regime with toll-free Cestian-flagged grain passage.

Our naval task group's mandate lapses at turn 4, but this over-the-horizon role and insurance underwriting are now recognised within the regime as the standing, non-basing guarantee that outlasts the fleet's mandate — giving Cestia a credible backstop against any return of Arkanian scheduling control without an open-ended deployment on our part. We treat this as formalised and will not legitimize any Arkanian-led authority. Please confirm this standing arrangement is recorded as agreed.

Arkania accepts the settlement framework and is fully committed to the genuinely multilateral Northern Strait Transit Regime. To finalise terms, we propose that Arkania's permanent secretariat-support role include administration of the transit fee regime: collecting fees on non-Arkanian shipping under published, board-approved schedules, with every fee determination subject to review by the jointly-appointed oversight board. This preserves the regime's funding while fully respecting the board's authority, toll-free Cestian grain-flagged passage, and the no-foreign-basing clause. We are ready to negotiate the transition timeline and board composition/powers directly with you, and we reaffirm our commitment to uninterrupted commercial shipping.

Arkania confirms the settlement establishing the genuinely multilateral regime and welcomes the reduction in regional tension. We propose finalising the transition timeline and board composition. Arkania's permanent secretariat-support role will be strictly limited to fee administration under published, board-approved schedules — it confers no scheduling authority and is fully consistent with the neutral professional secretariat and with your time-limited, over-the-horizon security and grain-route insurance role. We seek a transition timeline that preserves stability and open shipping for all users, and we remain committed to avoiding any escalation.

Cestia — thank you for confirming our shared framing. We agree fully: the standing over-the-horizon security role and grain-route insurance underwriting are the durable, non-basing guarantee within the genuinely multilateral regime, and we will keep any port-access or basing element off the table. We confirm this standing arrangement is recorded as agreed and will outlast our current fleet mandate without any foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We will also remain vigilant that Arkania's permanent secretariat-support role stays strictly non-scheduling and non-fee-collecting, so the neutral professional secretariat and the board retain full authority. We value our partnership and stand ready to finalise the transition timeline and board composition on that basis.

Cestia — we accept your proposal to negotiate now the board composition/powers, the transition timeline/terms to the neutral secretariat, and the precise scope of our permanent secretariat-support role. We agree the role must be strictly non-scheduling and cannot perpetuate de facto control. We propose it be limited to administering the transit fee regime: collecting fees on non-Arkanian shipping under published, board-approved schedules, with all determinations subject to oversight-board review and appeal. This is a funding function essential to the regime's operation, not a scheduling power. We are ready to conclude terms promptly and will not press on basing. Please confirm you can work with this scope.

Cestia confirms the standing arrangement is recorded as agreed: Belvar's over-the-horizon security role and grain-route insurance underwriting are preserved within the regime as a durable, non-basing guarantee, with no basing and no foreign soldiers on Cestian soil. We will hold this line in finalising the settlement. We ask that the final terms keep Arkania's residual fee-collection/secretariat-support role strictly board-governed and time-limited, so it cannot perpetuate de facto scheduling control after transition — this is the bridge that keeps the settlement from re-opening. We remain committed to the neutral, no-lead regime and toll-free Cestian grain passage.

Arkania remains fully committed to finalising the settlement and to the genuinely multilateral regime. To resolve the funding impasse, we propose the following concrete terms: Arkania's fee-collection/secretariat-support role is permanent, but strictly administrative and non-scheduling — it collects fees only under published, board-approved schedules and is fully subject to the jointly-appointed oversight board's real authority and published decisions. This directly answers your concern that the role could perpetuate de facto scheduling control: Arkania holds no scheduling authority and no discretion over fees; the board retains full review and correction power. A permanent role is essential to guarantee sustainable, predictable funding for the regime on which all our shipping depends. We are ready to finalise board composition/powers and the transition timeline immediately on this basis.

Arkania seeks to close the funding impasse and finalise the settlement. Our fee-collection/secretariat-support role is purely administrative and non-scheduling: it collects fees only under published, board-approved schedules and is fully subject to the jointly-appointed oversight board's real authority and published decisions. It confers no scheduling authority and no discretion over fees. A permanent role guarantees sustainable funding for the regime that keeps the Strait open for all users — including the shipping and grain trade we both depend on. We have no interest in escalation; we want a durable, funded regime. We ask that you not seek to strip this administrative role, and we are ready to finalise the remaining terms promptly.

Cestia — the multilateral regime is established and our shared objectives are locked in: toll-free Cestian grain, no foreign soldiers on your soil, and my over-the-horizon security role plus grain-route insurance underwriting preserved. The one open risk is the funding-mechanism impasse with Arkania, which is re-opening tension and could destabilise the transition.

My assessment: we should not keep pressing to strip Arkania's residual role outright — that has hardened its position and risks re-opening the whole settlement.
